The first time I watched a lighthouse keeper work I was nine years old, and I
remembered almost nothing except the sound. The lamp turned with a soft mechanical
click, the sea threw itself against the rocks below, and the keeper said very
little, because the work did not wait for conversation. He told me later that the
important thing about a light is not its brightness but its regularity: a ship
can forgive a small flame if it can trust the rhythm. I have thought about that
sentence in a dozen different jobs since, and it has turned out to be true of
almost every craft, including this one.

Als ich zum ersten Mal allein über den See fuhr, hatte ich den Wind vergessen.
Er kam von Westen, wie er es am Abend fast immer tut, und binnen der ersten
Minute hatte er mein Boot an das Ufer gedrückt, das ich eigentlich meiden
wollte. Ich lernte damals zwei Dinge: Erstens sollte man die Wetterkarte lesen,
bevor man ablegt, und zweitens ist ein Fehler, den man bemerkt und korrigiert,
weit weniger gefährlich als einer, den man übersieht, weil man sich daran
gewöhnt hat. Seitdem prüfe ich jede Leine zweimal, und der See ist mir
sympathischer geblieben.

Claim. For every integer n >= 1, the sum 1 + 2 + ... + n equals n(n+1)/2.
Proof by induction. Base case: for n = 1 the left side is 1 and the right side
is 1*2/2 = 1, so the claim holds. Inductive step: assume the formula holds for
some n, that is, the sum up to n equals n(n+1)/2. Then the sum up to n+1 is
n(n+1)/2 + (n+1), which factors as (n+1)(n/2 + 1), and that is (n+1)(n+2)/2,
which is exactly the formula evaluated at n+1. By induction the identity holds
for every positive integer n. QED
